'''Erika Tatiana Camacho''' is a Mexican and American mathematical biologist and professor of mathematics at the [[University of Texas at San Antonio]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sciences.utsa.edu/faculty/profiles/camacho-tatiana.html|title=Erika Tatiana Camacho, Ph.D.|website=sciences.utsa.edu|accessdate=11 April 2024|archive-date=26 May 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240526191205/https://sciences.utsa.edu/faculty/profiles/camacho-tatiana.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>
She is a 2014 [[Presidential Award for Excellence in Science, Mathematics, and Engineering Mentoring]] (PAESMEM) awardee.<ref name="paesmem">{{cite web|url=http://www.paesmem.com/node/2618/|title=PAESMEM Award|website=paesmem.net|access-date=2018-06-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180829124426/http://www.paesmem.com/node/2618/|archive-date=2018-08-29|url-status=dead}}</ref> She was taught and mentored in high school by [[Jaime Escalante]], who was the subject of the movie ''[[Stand and Deliver]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://thebestschools.org/magazine/jaime-escalante-21st-century-still-standing-delivering/|title=Jaime Escalante in the 21st Century: Still Standing and Delivering - The Best Schools|website=Thebestschools.org|accessdate=10 June 2018|archive-date=12 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612141715/https://thebestschools.org/magazine/jaime-escalante-21st-century-still-standing-delivering/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Education==
Camacho was born 3 September 1974, in Guadalajara, Mexico. She attended high school at [[Garfield High School (California)|Garfield High School]] from 1990 to 1993 where she was taught by [[Jaime Escalante]].<ref name="auto">{{cite web|url=http://math4science.org/erika-camacho/|title=Erika Camacho – Math4Science|website=Math4science.org|accessdate=10 June 2018|archive-date=12 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612140311/http://math4science.org/erika-camacho/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://diverseeducation.com/?emerging-scholar=life-in-absolute-values|title=Life In Absolute Values - Diverse|website=Diverseeducation.com|accessdate=10 June 2018}}</ref>  Being the first high school graduate in her family and a first generation college student. After graduating from [[Wellesley College]], cum laude, with [[Bachelor of Arts]] degrees in mathematics and economics in 1997, she went to earn a [[PhD]] in applied mathematics<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cam.cornell.edu/cam/about/spotlights.cfm?s_id=560&page=1|title=Spotlights - Center for Applied Mathematics - Cornell Engineering|website=Cam.cornell.edu|accessdate=10 June 2018}}</ref> at [[Cornell University]] in 2003 for her research on mathematical models of retinal dynamics. Camacho has also earned a Master of Science in Applied mathematics at Cornell University.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Erika Tatiana Camacho, Ph.D. {{!}} College of Sciences |url=https://sciences.utsa.edu/faculty/profiles/camacho-tatiana.html |access-date=2025-03-12 |website=sciences.utsa.edu |language=en-US |archive-date=2024-05-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240526191205/https://sciences.utsa.edu/faculty/profiles/camacho-tatiana.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Career ==
After spending a year as a postdoc at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]], Camacho joined the faculty of the Department of Mathematics at [[Loyola Marymount University]] in 2004. She co-founded and co-directed the summer [[Research Experiences for Undergraduates]], the Applied Mathematical Sciences Summer Research Institute (AMSSI), that ran from 2005 to 2007 with support from the [[National Science Foundation]] and the [[National Security Agency]]. Her research focuses on mathematical models of photoreceptors in the retina.<ref name="auto"/> In 2007, she moved to [[Arizona State University]] where she worked as a professor of [[applied mathematics]]. In 2013–2014, she taught at [[MIT]] in the MLK Visiting Scholars program.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://math.mit.edu/diversity/members/erika-camacho/|title=Erika Camacho, Mathematics – Martin Luther King Jr. Scholars|website=math.mit.edu|date=15 September 2021 |accessdate=20 Jan 2023}}</ref>  She has served on numerous national boards including the Council of the [[American Mathematical Society]] (AMS),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/about-us/governance/committees/council-past.html|title=AMS Council Members|website=ams.org|accessdate=20 Jan 2023}}</ref> the Advisory Board of [[National Institute for Mathematical and Biological Synthesis]] (NIMBioS),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nimbios.org/governance/|title=NIMBioS Board of Advisors|website=www.nimbios.org|accessdate=20 Jan 2023}}</ref> and [[Society for the Advancement of Chicanos/Hispanics and Native Americans in Science|SACNAS]] Board of Directors.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sacnas.org/board-of-directors|title=SACNAS Board of Directors|website=sacnas.org|accessdate=20 January 2023}}</ref> She served as an AMS Council member at large from 2018 to 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AMS Committees |url=http://www.ams.org/about-us/governance/committees/mal-past.html |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=American Mathematical Society |language=en}}</ref>

In September 2019 she began a 3-year rotation as a Program Director with the National Science Foundation. She was co-lead of the HSI Program and worked with the ADVANCE Program. She served as a Program Director in the Racial Equity in STEM Program Description where she and the other Program Directors were awarded a 2022 Director's Award for Superior Accomplishment: "For excellence, inclusion, collaboration, integrity, learning, transparency, and public service in creating and bringing to fruition the EHR Racial Equity in STEM Education Program Description, a timely idea whose impact may fundamentally change the scientific endeavor and NSF."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://events.tvworldwide.com/Events/NSF-Awards-Ceremony-2022|title=NSF Director's Award Ceremony|website=events.tvworldwide.com|accessdate=3 January 2023}}</ref>

Her first publication led to the discovery of rod-drive cone visibility factor. This discovery focused on RPE cell development.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Erika Tatiana Camacho {{!}} Women in Mathematics {{!}} University of Waterloo |url=https://uwaterloo.ca/women-in-mathematics/erika-tatiana-camacho |access-date=2025-09-29 |website=uwaterloo.ca |language=en}}</ref>  In January 2023, she began a Fulbright Scholar Award at the Institut de la Vision in Paris (Sorbonne University),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://fulbrightscholars.org/grantee/erika-camacho|title=U.S. Fulbright Scholar page}}</ref> 
<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.asu.edu/20220726-2-asu-math-professors-earn-prestigious-fulbright-scholar-awards|title=ASU math professors earn prestigious Fulbright Scholar Award|date=26 July 2022 }}</ref> and in August of that year, she announced her move to the University of Texas at San Antonio (UTSA).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.linkedin.com/posts/erika-tatiana-camacho-4665a013_i-am-at-the-university-of-texas-at-san-antonio-activity-7099428788068827136-IgO7/ |title=I am at The University of Texas at San Antonio!|date=August 2023 |website=linkedin.com |access-date=11 April 2024}}</ref> She is a Professor in the Department of Mathematics and in the Department of Neuroscience, Developmental and Regenerative Biology (NDRB) at UTSA. She holds the inaugural Manuel P. Berriozábal, Ph.D. and María Antonietta Berriozábal Endowed Chair.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.utsa.edu/endowed/profiles/manuel-maria-berriozabal-chair.html|title=UTSA Endowed and Named Chairs and Professorships}}</ref> She is also a staunch advocate for inclusivity in STEM.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://kjzz.org/content/446987/womens-business-conference-focus-latinas-stem-careers|title=Women's Business Conference To Focus On Latinas In STEM Careers|date=15 March 2017|website=KJZZ|accessdate=10 June 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://sloan-scholars.ssrc.org/sloan-scholars/spotlights-features/erika-camacho-on-mentoring-in-service-of-diversity/|title=Featured Interview: Sloan Scholar Erika Camacho on Mentoring in Service of Diversity – Sloan Scholars Mentoring Network|website=Sloan-scholars.ssrc.org|accessdate=10 June 2018|archive-date=2 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202063909/https://sloan-scholars.ssrc.org/sloan-scholars/spotlights-features/erika-camacho-on-mentoring-in-service-of-diversity/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.statepress.com/article/2010/03/asu-mathematics-professor-from-low-income-l-a-high-school-excelling-in-ariz/|title=Once uninspired student, math professor finds passion in teaching|website=Statepress.com|accessdate=10 June 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://technica-magazine.com/erika-tatiana-camacho-phd/|title=Erika Tatiana Camacho, Ph.D.|website=Technica Magazine|accessdate=10 June 2018|archive-date=12 June 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612143831/http://technica-magazine.com/erika-tatiana-camacho-phd/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Awards==
Camacho is the recipient of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]'s 2019 Mentor Award<ref>{{cite web |last1=Holland |first1=Richard |title=ASU New College professor receives 2019 AAAS Mentor Award |date=7 February 2019 |url=https://asunow.asu.edu/20190207-asu-new-college-professor-receives-2019-aaas-mentor-award |publisher=ASU Now |accessdate=9 February 2019}}</ref> and a 2014 [[Presidential Award for Excellence in Science, Mathematics, and Engineering Mentoring]] (PAESMEM),<ref name="paesmem"/> awarded for her research with and mentoring of undergraduates. In 2023 she received the [[M. Gweneth Humphreys Award]] in recognition of mathematics educators who have exhibited outstanding mentorship<ref>{{cite web|url=https://awm-math.org/2023-gweneth-humphreys-award/|title=Humphreys Award 2023|website=awm-math.org|date=19 October 2022 }}</ref> and in 2020 she received the [[Louise Hay Award]] for Mathematics Education,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://awm-math.org/awards/hay-award/hay-award-2020/|title=Hay Award 2020|website=awm-math.org}}</ref> both from the [[Association for Women in Mathematics]]. 

She won the 2020 [[Society for the Advancement of Chicanos/Hispanics and Native Americans in Science|SACNAS]] Presidential Service Award,<ref name=sacnas-award>{{cite web|url=https://www.sacnas.org/honor-excellence/archive|title=SACNAS Award|website=Sacnas.org|access-date=26 February 2024}}</ref> the 2018 [[American Association of Hispanics in Higher Education]] (AAHHE) Outstanding Latino/a Faculty in Higher Education Research/Teaching (Research Institutions) Award (now the AAHHE Sylvia Hurtado University Faculty Award),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aahhe.org/university-faculty-award|title=AAHHE Sylvia Hurtado University Faculty Award|publisher=American Association of Hispanics in Higher Education|access-date=2024-06-17}}</ref> the 2017 HENAAC Education Award,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.greatmindsinstem.org/professionals/award-winners-2017.html|title=award-winners-2017|website=Greatmindsinstem.org|access-date=2017-11-17|archive-date=2021-07-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210729054619/https://www.greatmindsinstem.org/professionals/award-winners-2017.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> the 2012 [[Society for the Advancement of Chicanos/Hispanics and Native Americans in Science|SACNAS]] Distinguished Undergraduate Institution Mentor Award,<ref name=sacnas-award/> and the 2011 Hispanic Women's Corporation National Latina Leadership Award.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://azpbs.org/horizonte/2011/09/hispanic-womens-conference/|title=Hispanic Women's Conference - Arizona PBS|website=Azpbs.org}}</ref> In 2012, Camacho also received the 40 Hispanic Leaders Under 40 Award in Phoenix.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mathematician Erika Camacho receives national, local awards {{!}} ASU News |url=https://news.asu.edu/content/mathematician-erika-camacho-receives-national-local-awards |access-date=2025-09-21 |website=news.asu.edu}}</ref>

Camacho was selected a Fellow of the [[Association for Women in Mathematics]] in the class of 2024 "for her leadership in the advancement, mentoring, and support of women and underrepresented groups at all levels through the creation of opportunities, collaborative research, and impactful service. Her work brings sustained systemic change, diversity, equity, and inclusion in mathematics, and more broadly in STEM."<ref name="Association for Women in Mathematics (AWM) b931">{{cite web | title=2024 AWM Fellows | website=Association for Women in Mathematics (AWM) | url=https://awm-math.org/awards/awm-fellows/2024-awm-fellows/ | access-date=28 October 2023}}</ref> She  was elected as a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]] in the 2024 class of fellows.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/fellows_by_year.cgi?year=2024|title=2024 Class of Fellows of the AMS|publisher=American Mathematical Society|access-date=8 November 2023}}</ref>
